strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 37 tasks (Adroit + Meta-World) with 3 random seeds, covering multiple strong baselines including DP3, FlowPolicy, and the closely related MP1
The gradient analysis in Section 4.2 (Eqs. 5-7) provides a clear, plausible geometric motivation for why MSE-trained flow models underperform on low-velocity, high-precision manipulation tasks
The proposed OMP shows meaningful gains on the hardest task categories (e.g., +10.6% over MP1 on Meta-World Very Hard tasks), which is where improvements matter most
The ablation study (Table 2) isolates each component, and the training curves in Figure 4 support claims of improved stability and convergence
Related work is thorough and positions the contribution clearly relative to MP1 and DM1
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the 'Directional Alignment' is a standard cosine-similarity loss, and the 'Differential Derivation Equation' (Eq. 11) is simply a finite-difference approximation of a derivative presented under a new name, without any analysis of approximation error or sensitivity to the perturbation constant epsilon

Potential correctness issue in Eq. 11: the MeanFlow Identity (Eq. 4) involves the total derivative d/dt of u(z_t, r, t), which should account for the change of z_t with t along the trajectory, but the finite-difference scheme perturbs only t while holding z_t fixed; this discrepancy is not discussed and could undermine the DDE proposal

The abstract claims improved 'few-shot generalization' and criticizes MP1's fixed temperature hyperparameters in the Dispersive Loss, but the paper presents no dedicated few-shot generalization experiments and never addresses the temperature issue in the method
The paper is simulation-only (Adroit and Meta-World); no real-robot experiments are provided, limiting evidence for the claimed practical value for 'real-time control'
Reproducibility gaps: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (lambda_cos, lambda_Disp, epsilon in Eq. 11, network architecture) are not specified

Ablation results contain unexplained anomalies: the '-JVP + DDE' variant outperforms full OMP on Adroit Pen (64 vs. 60), and the average improvement over MP1 (3.4%) is within roughly one standard deviation, so the headline claim rests mainly on the harder task subsets

The theoretical motivation (gradient starvation for small-magnitude targets) is asserted rather than empirically verified; e.g., no experiment isolates low-velocity regimes to show cosine loss specifically helps there

Writing quality is below bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos ('twnety-one', 'decoder decoderθ', 'Mean Policy' in Figure 2, inconsistent 'mp1/MP1'), a garbled sentence in Section 4 opening, and Eq. 11 contains an apparent typo in its arguments

Several key baselines and related methods (MP1, DM1, World4RL, TRDRL, CLAP) are arXiv-only 2025 preprints, and it is unclear whether Table 1 numbers are reproduced or copied, which affects comparability

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practically relevant problem: reducing the inference latency of generative robot policies while improving success rates, building on the recent MeanFlow framework.

Empirical gains over the closest baseline (MP1) are non-trivial on the more difficult Meta-World splits (e.g., +9.4% on Medium, +10.6% on Very Hard tasks), while preserving single-step (NFE=1) inference.
The gradient analysis of the MSE loss (Eqs. 5-7), decomposing error into radial and tangential components, is a reasonably interesting (if heuristic) motivation for a directional loss term.
An ablation study over the proposed components is included, and the evaluation protocol (3 seeds, multiple task difficulty tiers, explicit NFE reporting) is laid out transparently.
weaknesses: Technical soundness of the DDE contribution is questionable. The MeanFlow identity (Eq. 4) requires the *total* time derivative d/dt u(zt, r, t|c), which includes the dependence of the output on zt as it moves along the trajectory. Eq. 11 only finite-differences the explicit t argument while holding zt fixed, i.e., it approximates the partial derivative, not the JVP it is meant to replace. The paper neither acknowledges nor analyzes this discrepancy, and the equation itself is malformed (the second term reads uθ(zt, t, ε, r|c), with ε inserted in the wrong argument position).

Central claims are not supported by the presented evidence. The abstract and introduction claim improved 'few-shot generalization' and 'trajectory accuracy', yet no few-shot ablation (varying demonstration counts) and no trajectory-error metrics are reported. Similarly, the JVP-replacement is motivated by GPU memory savings, but no memory measurements or training-time comparisons (DDE vs. JVP) are provided anywhere—the claimed trade-off is never quantified.

The theoretical motivation for the Cosine Loss is shaky. Aligning the predicted *interval-averaged* velocity u(zt, r, t|c) with the straight-line vector v0 = zT − z0 (Eq. 3) is only valid for the conditional straight-line path; the marginal average velocity over an arbitrary [r, t] interval is not generally collinear with v0. Forcing this alignment for all (r, t) may conflict with the MeanFlow identity target, and the paper does not analyze or empirically isolate this potential conflict.

The 'gradient starvation' argument is weak: when ρ* → 0 the direction of the target is ill-defined, so vanishing directional gradient there is arguably appropriate rather than pathological; the paper offers no direct empirical measurement of this phenomenon on the actual tasks.

Evaluation is limited to simulation (3 Adroit + 34 Meta-World tasks), only 3 random seeds, and the overall margin over MP1 is 3.4% with overlapping variance bands in places; no real-robot experiments are included.

Reproducibility is poor: no code release, and key hyperparameters (λcos, λDisp, ε, network architecture) are unspecified. It is also unclear which baseline numbers were re-run versus copied, and the strongest baselines (MP1, DM1) are themselves arXiv preprints.

Presentation quality is below bar: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('twnety-one', 'increase attention', 'decoder decoderθ'), a partially garbled Eq. 11, an incomplete Background section (e.g., misplaced sentences in the flow-matching and one-step-model paragraphs), and Section 4.2 ends mid-sentence into a run-on heading.

strengths: Clear positioning of the problem: one-step generative policies for robot manipulation are practically motivated, and the paper identifies concrete weaknesses of MP1 (directional drift of predicted velocities, GPU memory cost of the JVP operator).

The geometric analysis of the MSE loss (Eq. 5–7) is a nice, intuitive motivation: showing that the gradient signal for correcting directional error vanishes as target velocity magnitude shrinks gives a plausible account of why flow-based policies underperform on fine-grained tasks.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad (37 tasks across Adroit and Meta-World, 3 random seeds, multiple baselines including DP3, Simple DP3, FlowPolicy, MP1), and the reported gains are concentrated on the harder Meta-World task groups (e.g., +10.6% on Very Hard), which is where improvements matter most.
The ablation study isolates the proposed components and the training-curves analysis (Fig. 4) supports claims of improved stability and convergence.
Single-step inference (NFE=1) with strong average success rates (82.3%) and real-time control frequency is a practically useful operating point.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is thin: a cosine-similarity loss and a finite-difference approximation of the JVP are both standard, well-known techniques. The novelty over MP1 (Sheng et al., 2025) and DM1 (Zou et al., 2025) is incremental, and DM1 — explicitly identified as closely related — is discussed but never compared against experimentally.

There is a serious soundness concern with the DDE (Eq. 11). The MeanFlow identity requires the total derivative d/dt u(z_t, r, t) (Eq. 4), which in practice is the JVP of the network output with respect to z_t along the velocity field. A finite difference taken only in t, as written in Eq. 11, approximates ∂u/∂t, not the Jacobian-vector product w.r.t. z_t. The equation also appears malformed (a stray ε inside the second argument, and the numerator does not correspond to a correct central difference u(t+ε) − u(t−ε)). As written, the key technical claim of Section 4.4 is not substantiated; the actual implementation is not described precisely enough to verify.

The paper does not analyze the interaction between the proposed Cosine Loss and the MeanFlow identity. Forcing u(z_t, r, t|c) to align with the straight-line vector v0 = z_T − z_0 could conflict with the identity's target u_tgt (Eq. 4), especially for multimodal demonstrations where the optimal flow path is not a straight line. No theory or experiment addresses this tension. Moreover, the cosine is ill-defined when the predicted velocity norm approaches zero — precisely the low-velocity regime the paper claims to fix — and no numerical stabilization is discussed.

Central claims are not supported by the experiments presented. The abstract claims the method 'effectively enhances few-shot generalization,' yet no few-shot or generalization experiment is reported; all evaluations use the same 10 demonstrations per task. Similarly, memory savings of DDE are asserted but never quantified.

The evaluation protocol is favorable to the proposed method: final performance is computed as 'the average of the five highest success rates' over periodic evaluations, which is effectively best-checkpoint cherry-picking. With only 3 seeds and standard deviations of ~2%, the headline 3.4% average improvement over MP1 is fragile, and no statistical significance testing is provided.

The ablations are confounded: the directional-alignment component is only ablated jointly with removal of the dispersive loss (−L_dis − L_cos), so its isolated contribution relative to the full OMP (rather than relative to OMP minus two components) is unclear. Notably, the fully ablated model (78.3%) is worse than MP1 (78.9%), suggesting most of OMP's advantage may come from tuning rather than the proposed components.

Reproducibility is inadequate: key hyperparameters (λ_cos, λ_disp, ε) are never specified, no code release is mentioned, and the paper lacks a limitations discussion. All experiments are simulation-only (Adroit/Meta-World); no real-robot results despite the paper's framing around 'high-precision robotic manipulation.'

Presentation has numerous defects that undermine trust: Eq. 11 is malformed, typos throughout ('twnety-one', 'decoder decoderθ', 'Mean Policy' vs. MeanFlow in Fig. 2), inconsistent naming (mp1/MP1, Flowpolicy), Figure 1 reports FPS without per-method latency numbers for OMP, and baselines include citations formatted inconsistently (e.g., 'MP1(arxiv'25)').

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 3 Adroit tasks, 34 Meta-World tasks (3 seeds each), and 3 real-world manipulation tasks with 20 trials, comparing against a broad set of recent baselines (DP/DP3, Simple DP3, FlowPolicy, MPI1, CP, AdaFlow) at matched NFE settings.

Clear identification and motivation of three candidate failure modes of MeanFlow applied to robotics (spectral attenuation of the averaged-velocity target, direction/magnitude coupling of MSE in low-velocity regimes, and ~2x activation memory from nested JVP differentiation), each supported by a controlled synthetic experiment or memory measurement (Fig. 2, Table 3, Appendix B/C).

Useful memory analysis (Appendix B.3) showing the JVP-based total derivative roughly doubles activation memory, and a practical finite-difference (DDE) variant that cuts GPU memory substantially (e.g., 26.7GB to 19.2GB) with only a ~1.5% average success-rate drop.

Thorough ablations isolating the Dispersive and Directional Alignment loss terms, plus a sensitivity study over action-chunk horizons (Table 5), and generally good reproducibility details (hyperparameters in Table 4, seeds, training budgets, code in supplementary).
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is heuristic and in places technically flawed. Theorem B.1 treats the averaging operator as pure integration (|U(w)| ~ |V(w)|/|w|), ignoring the time-varying 1/t normalization, so the claimed quadratic PSD decay of the average-velocity target is not rigorously established for the actual MeanFlow target. Similarly, the 'gradient starvation' argument (Eq. 8-9) is a 2D polar-coordinate decomposition; in the Cartesian parametrization networks actually use, the Euclidean gradient does not vanish as rho* -> 0, so the transfer of this pathology to high-dimensional deep policies is asserted rather than demonstrated beyond the toy experiment.

Methodological novelty is limited: the Directional Alignment loss is a standard cosine-similarity auxiliary term, and the DDE is a finite-difference approximation of the JVP borrowed from prior work (Wang et al. 2025c). The contribution is largely an empirical combination of these ingredients on top of MeanFlow.

The 'critical pathology' narrative is undermined by the results: MPI1, which the authors argue suffers from exactly these pathologies, still achieves 78.9% average success vs. OMP's 82.3%. The improvement is modest relative to reported standard deviations (~1.7-2.1%), only 3 seeds are used, and no statistical significance testing is provided.

The DDE approximation introduces finite-difference bias, but the perturbation epsilon is never analyzed or ablated; the cited 'sensitivity analysis in Section E' concerns action-chunk lengths, not epsilon, leaving a key hyperparameter of the proposed method unjustified.

Internal inconsistencies and overclaiming: the conclusion cites 'Numerical Instability in Short-Horizon Denoising' as an analyzed pathology, which does not appear in the paper; phrases like 'rigorous analysis' and 'establishing a new standard' exceed what the evidence supports.

Figure 1's speed-success comparison does not control for backbone/representation differences across methods, so the FPS axis conflates architecture choices with the proposed objective; real-world evaluation is limited to three tasks with one robot setup.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: 37 simulation tasks across Adroit and Meta-World with 3 random seeds, plus real-world experiments on 3 physical tasks, with ablations of both loss components (Table 1) and a JVP-vs-DDE memory/accuracy trade-off analysis (Tables 3, 5).

The paper attempts to ground its design choices in analysis rather than pure engineering: the low-pass-filter argument for the averaging operator (Thm B.1), the polar decomposition of the MSE gradient (Eq. 19-21), and the memory-doubling derivation for nested JVP backprop (B.3) are supported by small controlled synthetic experiments (Figure 2, Appendix C).

The proposed modifications are lightweight and practically motivated; the directional alignment loss and finite-difference derivative are simple to implement, and the reported training-stability curves (Figure 5) suggest a real benefit over baselines.
The limitations of the DDE approximation are honestly quantified (a 1.5-point average drop, Table 1) rather than hidden, and the memory-savings justification is given concretely (Table 3).
weaknesses: Limited originality: both core components are combinations of existing techniques — the directional loss is a standard cosine-similarity auxiliary objective applied on top of MP1/DM1, and the DDE is explicitly a finite-difference JVP approximation borrowed from prior work (Karakida et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2025c). The headline gain over the closest baseline MP1 is modest (~3.4% average) and statistical significance is never established with only 3 seeds and overlapping standard deviations.

The theoretical analysis is heuristic rather than rigorous, and at least one central claim appears internally inconsistent: the Directional Alignment loss (Eq. 12) aligns the interval-averaged velocity u(z_t, r, t|c) with v0 = z_T − z_0 (Eq. 3), which is the full-interval mean velocity — these quantities coincide only when (r, t) spans the whole trajectory, yet training samples random intervals. Moreover, cosine similarity is undefined/unstable as ||v0|| → 0, directly contradicting the claim that the gradient 'remains non-zero even when ||v0|| → 0'.

Equation (14), the central DDE formula, is garbled (uθ(z_t, t, ε, r|c)) and mathematically inconsistent: (u(t+ε) − u(t))/(2ε) is not a central difference — a central difference requires evaluating at t+ε and t−ε. No error analysis or justification of the perturbation constant ε is provided.

The narrative is inconsistent with itself: the Conclusion cites 'Numerical Instability in Short-Horizon Denoising' as a key identified pathology, which is never analyzed anywhere in the paper; Section 5.1 states '4 tasks in real-world setting' but then describes 3; the claimed mechanism by which DA 'circumvents' spectral bias is asserted but never demonstrated.

The gradient-starvation argument (ρ* → 0 gives zero angular gradient) is a property of MSE regression in general, not specific to MeanFlow, and the motivating tasks ('Peg Insertion', 'Thread in Hole') are never actually evaluated — the empirical validation is limited to a 2D toy experiment with a frozen output vector, so the link between the theory and the benchmark gains remains speculative.

The real-world evaluation is too small to support the claims of 'substantial' gains: 20 trials per task means the 10-15% improvements over MP1 correspond to 2-3 additional successes, with no confidence intervals.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: typos ('twnety-one', 'real-word'), a mismatched Figure 3 legend ('Mean Policy'), unfinished sentences (Section 4.2.3 'the computational burden .'), and unclear baseline provenance (MP1 cited as 'AAAI'26').

strengths: The paper identifies and analyzes three concrete failure modes (spectral bias from the averaging operator, gradient starvation in low-velocity regimes, and memory cost of nested JVP differentiation) when applying MeanFlow to robot policies. The motivating analyses, including the synthetic sum-of-sines experiment (Fig. 2a, Theorem B.1) and the controlled 2D angular-error experiment (Fig. 2b, Eq. 8-9, B.2), are thoughtful and give the empirical design choices a clear rationale.

The evaluation is broad: 6 Adroit tasks plus 34 Meta-World tasks with 3 random seeds, sensitivity analysis over action-chunk lengths, a loss-component ablation, GPU-memory measurements (Table 3), and three real-robot tasks. The proposed OMP outperforms strong one-step baselines (MPI, FlowPolicy) on average (82.3% vs 78.9% for MPI-JVP on simulation) while retaining NFE=1.

The JVP vs. DDE comparison is honest: the authors report that the finite-difference approximation incurs a measurable performance drop (82.3% -> 80.8%) in exchange for substantial memory savings, and they analyze when each variant is preferable (Table 5).
The paper is generally well organized, with preliminary experiments (Appendix C) that directly validate each claimed pathology before introducing the method.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest and components are assembled from prior work. MPI (Sheng et al., 2025) already applies MeanFlow to manipulation; the Directional Alignment loss is a standard cosine-similarity auxiliary objective, and the DDE is a finite-difference approximation explicitly borrowed from prior work (Wang et al., 2025c; Karakida et al., 2023). The contribution is essentially an incremental refinement of MPI, and the paper's framing as a 'theoretical breakthrough' level advance overstates this.

The claimed improvement over the strongest baseline is small relative to the evaluation noise. On Meta-World Easy tasks MPI already achieves 88.2% vs. OMP's 89.7%; the headline gap is 3.4% average with no statistical significance testing. Real-world gains (10-15%) are based on only 20 trials per task across 3 tasks, which does not establish significance.

The evaluation metric ('top-5 average success' over evaluations every 200 epochs) selects the best checkpoints, which can inflate reported numbers; standard final-checkpoint or last-k averages would be more trustworthy. This protocol detail is easy to miss and weakens comparability with prior reports.

The theory is heuristic rather than rigorous. Theorem B.1 assumes wide-sense stationary velocity processes, an assumption poorly matched to piecewise manipulation trajectories; the gradient-starvation analysis concerns a single 2D vector with frozen weights, and no analysis connects these idealized settings quantitatively to the actual policy-learning losses.

Internal inconsistency: the Conclusion cites 'Numerical Instability in Short-Horizon Denoising' as an identified pathology, but this is never analyzed in the paper (the intro lists spectral bias, gradient starvation, and memory complexity). This suggests rushed writing and undermines confidence in the claims.

Several reproducibility details are missing: loss weights (lambda_dis, lambda_DA) in Eq. 13 are never specified, the finite-difference perturbation epsilon is not given, and no guidance is provided on tuning them; code is only 'included in supplementary material' without stated licensing or verification.
Figure 1 reports ~120 FPS for OMP but the control-frequency measurement protocol (what is timed, per what hardware, with which encoder) is not described, making the efficiency claims hard to verify.

The real-world evaluation (3 tasks, single robot setup) is limited, and the claimed robustness on 'Slip Ring' (40-55% success) still leaves substantial headroom; broader real-robot validation would be needed to support the 'new standard for real-time generative robot control' claim.
